analysisDescription: To analyze this game, I tried to look at important categories like teamwork and communication and chose options that best represent how the game works and found examples of these in action, such as using voice chat and working together on tasks. I also examined how these elements interact and affect player behavior, providing clear examples for each. In the end, this analysis showed how crucial teamwork and communication are for success in the game, giving a clear understanding of player interactions and mechanics.

dimensionExamples.example: Players can create parties before entering a match, by inviting friends to join a party directly from the main menu.

dimension.title: Party Creation
dimension.description: Party Creation encompasses all games where groups are defined by the players themselves prior to initiating gameplay, typically leveraging friend lists or co-located party creation.

dimensionExamples.example: Allows players to post requests for teammates in the game's matchmaking interface, or start a new game in order to join a server with a group formed already.

dimension.title: Looking for Group
dimension.description: Looking for Group happens when there are grouping mechanisms that allow players to formally look for and create a group/party. This is typically achieved through matchmaking or looking for group queues.

dimensionExamples.example: Occurs in competitive play where teams often use external communication tools, like Discord, to strategize and coordinate before matches.

dimension.title: Organised Grouping
dimension.description: Organised Grouping covers all features that establish groups/communities (e.g. guilds) within games, which typically persist across different gaming sessions and may have defined roles and/or hierarchy.

dimensionExamples.example: All players on the team share the common objective of winning the match, whether it's planting or defusing a bomb, or securing hostage rescue.

dimension.title: Shared
dimension.description: Shared goals consist of singular objectives that multiple players pursue and work together to achieve

dimensionExamples.example: The goals of each players are often intertwined. For example, while one player may focus on planting the bomb, others might need to protect them or eliminate enemies.

dimension.title: Intertwined
dimension.description: Intertwined goals determine individual objectives assigned to different players that, in some way, are dependent on each other. The dependency may be uni- or bidirectional. If the dependency is bidirectional, goals are interdependent.

dimensionExamples.example: Within a team, players can also have conflicting personal goals, such as wanting to achieve individual goals (like getting the most kills) versus working as a cohesive unit to win the match.

dimension.title: Conflicting
dimension.description: Conflicting goals are also observable in some cooperative games, where typically, players compete in certain sections that do not affect the overarching goal of the game. While no semi-cooperative games were observed, in these types of games, conflicting goals can also be mixed with shared goals

dimensionExamples.example: In Counter-Strike 2, the community plays a significant role in player progression. Players can engage with others, sharing strategies, tips, and experiences that help them improve.

dimension.title: Community
dimension.description: Community progression is defined by the joint efforts of players in a larger community (e.g. guilds, factions, or even an entire player base) that, while not necessarily playing together, can contribute to typically shared consequences.

dimensionExamples.example: Each player can track their own performance metrics, such as kill/death ratios and win rates. Players progress by improving their skills and gaining ranks, which directly impacts their gameplay experience and status in the game.

dimension.title: Individual
dimension.description: Individual progression is defined by individual choice and the individual impact of the progression. In-game activities can vary from individual to fully cooperative but progression affects the individual.

dimensionExamples.example: In Counter-Strike 2, players often develop a distinct identity through their chosen roles, playstyles, and strategies.

dimension.title: Distinct
dimension.description: Distinct means that each player controls a different entity or set of entities

dimensionExamples.example: There is a shared identity among team members based on their common goal of winning matches. Also professional and amateur teams have often an identity

dimension.title: Shared
dimension.description: Shared applies when input from multiple players directly translates to the actions of one playable entity

dimensionExamples.example: Players in Counter-Strike 2 can customize their experience extensively, from choosing weapon skins and character models to adjusting game settings.

dimension.title: Customisation
dimension.description: Customisation applies when players select their identity by creating or modifying (with a certain degree of freedom) the play style of an entity.

dimensionExamples.example: Player progression is predefined through a ranking system where players advance based on their performance in matches.

dimension.title: Predefined
dimension.description: When progress is strictly linear, with no player choice (e.g., dictated by the storyline, predefined upgrades or progressing through switching entities)

dimensionExamples.example: Players work together as teammates to achieve common objectives, such as planting or defusing bombs. A good cooperation among teammates is important for a good performance in a match

dimension.title: Teammates
dimension.description: Teammates, where players within a team need to coordinate their actions, abilities, and roles in order to reach a common goal against at least another team.

dimensionExamples.example: While players collaborate with their teammates, they are also competitors against the opposing team.

dimension.title: Competitors
dimension.description: Competitors, where you may be able to compete with other players, either momentarily or through the whole game session (e.g. team vs team match-based games).

dimensionExamples.example: The game world is shared among all players in a match, with the same maps and objectives.

dimension.title: Shared
dimension.description: Shared world views apply to a game when players have access to the same world.

dimensionExamples.example: Players share a common perspective in that everyone views the same game objectives, rules and maps.

dimension.title: Shared
dimension.description: Shared is when there is a single viewpoint that both players share. Typically, this happens when players are co-located. All Shared Player Views are, by definition, in Shared Game Worlds.

dimensionExamples.example: Each player can experience is distinct due to individual point of view during a match. They can also have different strategies and play-styles

dimension.title: Distinct
dimension.description: Distinct refers to when each player has control of their own individual viewpoint, typically through separate screens.

dimensionExamples.example: Strict collaboration occurs when teammates coordinate their actions closely, such as executing a planned strategy or attack.

dimension.title: Strict Collaboration
dimension.description: In strict collaboration, the game assigns specific tasks to players, with players having little freedom to shape their interaction.

dimensionExamples.example: Coupled collaboration is seen when players work alongside each other but may not be strictly coordinating every action.

dimension.title: Coincident Collaboration
dimension.description: In coincident collaboration, players are accomplishing the same task together.

dimensionExamples.example: Concurrent collaboration is put to use when players execute actions simultaneously during a set in a match.

dimension.title: Concurrent Collaboration
dimension.description: In concurrent collaboration, players have to perform gameplay tasks concurrently.

dimensionExamples.example: Sequential collaboration is used when players take turns executing their roles in a strategy. For example, one player throws a smoke grenade while another player waits for it to plant the bomb.

dimension.title: Sequential Collaboration
dimension.description: In sequential collaboration, players have to do tasks in sequential order, with tasks typically assigned to different players.

dimensionExamples.example: Players are incentivized to communicate to share information about enemy positions, strategies, and game objectives in order to succeed

dimension.title: Required/Incentivised
dimension.description: When Required/Incentivised, the game challenges require players to communicate (e.g. when there is essential asymmetric information), or incentivised through challenges that are made easier through it (e.g. coordinating combined actions for maximum effect).

dimensionExamples.example: During a match, there is a public chat, where you can either talk to your team or to the opponents as well

dimension.title: Text Chat
dimension.description: Support for players to communicate using text

dimensionExamples.example: The ping system allows players to mark different locations in the map, without using text or voice messages.

dimension.title: Pings
dimension.description: Support for players to communicate by signaling specific things in their view (e.g. aiming at something and signaling)

dimensionExamples.example: Voice chat is the primary source of communication during a match, because teammates can share information quickly, and plan some strategies.

dimension.title: Voice Chat
dimension.description: Support for players to communicate using their voice

dimensionExamples.example: Task dependencies are evident as players rely on each other to complete specific roles. For instance, one player might be responsible for providing cover while another plants the bomb.

dimension.title: Task
dimension.description: Task refers to gameplay tasks where at least one player is dependent on another. These can force players to coordinate to be effective and complete them.

dimensionExamples.example: Players must coordinate their positioning relative to each other and the environment.

dimension.title: Spatial
dimension.description: Spatial, inspired by Reuter et al. 2014, happens when the game forces or incentivises players to be at a certain distance from one another. This can happen in a variety of ways, for example, by creating a radius around which players cannot trespass or by designing mechanics that punish players that move too far away from the group.

dimensionExamples.example: Assistive actions are common, where players help their teammates by providing support, such as covering fire, or throwing utility items like smoke grenades to obscure vision.

dimension.title: Assistive Actions
dimension.description: Assistive Actions encompass actions that one player performs to the benefit of other/s (i.e. note that the player can have indirect benefits such as reviving others to increase their own chances of success). In these games, players can support and assist other players in achieving their objectives.

dimensionExamples.example: Players can manipulate the game environment in order to gain advantage on the opponents.

dimension.title: Manipulating Others' entities
dimension.description: Manipulating Others' entities is a specific type of assistive action that refers to situations where a player can directly control or manipulate the actions, movements, or abilities of another player's character. This can lead to cooperative gameplay dynamics or just playful interactions.

dimensionExamples.example: Players can share consumables like granades, smokes and flashbangs, and coordinate to ensure these items are available to the players that need it to perform a specific strategy.

dimension.title: Consumables
dimension.description: Consumables refer to items that exist in a limited amount and can be utilised by players to invoke an effect (usually existing as a form of currency, materials, or food) or are not consumed on purpose by players but support the gameplay (e.g., health, energy). Consumables are shared when the agency to consume and manage them pertains to more than one player.

dimensionExamples.example: Different roles can vary the usefulness in different situations. For example, a sniper can be useful with covering something long distance, or a player that knows different strategies on smoke position can be useful while planting a bomb.

dimension.title: Usefulness
dimension.description: Usefulness happens when a certain resource or information (shared among multiple players) is more valuable  to one of those players. It can promote collaboration and coordination to maximise player performance/enjoyment.

dimensionExamples.example: Synergies are evident when players combine their abilities and actions to create a stronger overall effect

dimension.title: Synergies
dimension.description: Synergies extended from Rocha et. al 2008 allow one entity to assist or change the game actions (e.g. abilities) of another.

dimensionExamples.example: Complementarity refers to how different roles and actions enhance one another.

dimension.title: Complementarity
dimension.description: Complementarity, extended from Rocha et. al rocha2008game, corresponds to when player actions are designed to balance each other’s weaknesses or so that strengths complement each other. It is typically achieved through asymmetric game design, with each player bringing something to the shared experience.
